					<div id="mw-content-text" class="mw-body-content"><div class="mw-content-ltr mw-parser-output" lang="en" dir="ltr" data-mw-parsoid-version="0.24.0.0-alpha24" data-mw-html-version="2.8.0"><section data-mw-section-id="0" id="mwAQ"><div class="shortdescription nomobile noexcerpt noprint searchaux" style="display:none" about="#mwt1" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAg" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Short description","href":"./Template:Short_description"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Sunbeams that originate when the Sun appears to be just below the horizon"}},"i":0}}]}">Sunbeams that originate when the Sun appears to be just below the horizon</div><span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt1"><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_with_short_description"><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Short_description_is_different_from_Wikidata"></span>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwAw"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sun_over_Lake_Hawea,_New_Zealand.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwBA"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sun_over_Lake_Hawea,_New_Zealand.jpg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Sun_over_Lake_Hawea%2C_New_Zealand.jpg/330px-Sun_over_Lake_Hawea%2C_New_Zealand.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Sun_over_Lake_Hawea%2C_New_Zealand.jpg/960px-Sun_over_Lake_Hawea%2C_New_Zealand.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail 2x" data-file-width="7784" data-file-height="3236" data-file-type="bitmap" height="129" width="310" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 1.25" id="mwBQ"></a><figcaption id="mwBg"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunlight" title="Sunlight" id="mwBw">Sunlight</a> shining through <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud" title="Cloud" id="mwCA">clouds</a>, giving rise to crepuscular rays over <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Hāwea" title="Lake Hāwea" id="mwCQ">Lake Hāwea</a>, New Zealand</figcaption></figure>

<p id="mwCg"><b id="mwCw">Crepuscular rays</b>, sometimes colloquially known as <b id="mwDA">god rays</b>, <b id="mwDQ">twilight rays</b>, or <b id="mwDg">Jacob's ladder</b>, are visible shafts of sunlight that originate when the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun" title="Sun" id="mwDw">Sun</a> appears to be just above or below a layer of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud" title="Cloud" id="mwEA">clouds</a>, during the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilight" title="Twilight" id="mwEQ">twilight</a> period.<sup about="#mwt5" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-1"}}"><a href="#cite_note-1" id="mwEg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwEw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwFA">[</span>1<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwFQ">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt8" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-2"}}"><a href="#cite_note-2" id="mwFg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwFw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwGA">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwGQ">]</span></span></a></sup> Crepuscular rays are often observed as visible light beams passing through gaps in clouds, and are especially prominent when the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contrast_(vision)" title="Contrast (vision)" id="mwGg">contrast</a> between light and dark is most obvious.<sup about="#mwt11" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-3" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-3"}}"><a href="#cite_note-3" id="mwGw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwHA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwHQ">[</span>3<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwHg">]</span></span></a></sup> The term "crepuscular" comes from the Latin word <i lang="la" about="#mwt2" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwHw" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"wikt-lang","href":"./Template:Wikt-lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"la"},"2":{"wt":"crepusculum"}},"i":0}}]}"><a rel="mw:WikiLink/Interwiki" href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/crepusculum#Latin" title="wikt:crepusculum" class="extiw">crepusculum</a></i>, meaning "twilight".<sup about="#mwt14" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-4" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-4"}}"><a href="#cite_note-4" id="mwIA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwIQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwIg">[</span>4<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwIw">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwJA">During twilight, Crepuscular rays can commonly exhibit an orange or reddish coloration. This is due to the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rayleigh_scattering" title="Rayleigh scattering" id="mwJQ">Rayleigh scattering</a> phenomenon, in which as light travels through the atmosphere, it encounters particles and gases which scatters short-wavelength (blue) light more strongly than longer wavelengths (orange and red). During <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn" title="Dawn" id="mwJg">dawn</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dusk" title="Dusk" id="mwJw">dusk</a>, sunlight travels at low solar angles and through a greater thickness of the atmosphere - about 40 times more air than when the Sun is overhead at midday - resulting in a more pronounced warm colouration in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunbeam" title="Sunbeam" id="mwKA">sunbeams</a>.<sup about="#mwt17" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-5" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-5"}}"><a href="#cite_note-5" id="mwKQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwKg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwKw">[</span>5<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwLA">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwLQ">Crepuscular rays are in fact almost parallel to one another; however they appear to radiate outwards, due to a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perspective_(graphical)" title="Perspective (graphical)" id="mwLg">perspective</a> effect, similar to how parallel lines of a long road appear to meet in the distance.<sup about="#mwt20" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-6" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-6"}}"><a href="#cite_note-6" id="mwLw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwMA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwMQ">[</span>6<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwMg">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt23" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-7" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-7"}}"><a href="#cite_note-7" id="mwMw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwNA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwNQ">[</span>7<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwNg">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt26" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-8" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-8"}}"><a href="#cite_note-8" id="mwNw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwOA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwOQ">[</span>8<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwOg">]</span></span></a></sup> Loosely, the term <i id="mwOw">crepuscular rays</i> is sometimes extended to the general phenomenon of rays of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunlight" title="Sunlight" id="mwPA">sunlight</a> that appear to converge at a point in the sky, irrespective of time of day.<sup about="#mwt29" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-9" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-9"}}"><a href="#cite_note-9" id="mwPQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwPg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwPw">[</span>9<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwQA">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt32" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-10" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-10"}}"><a href="#cite_note-10" id="mwQQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwQg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwQw">[</span>10<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwRA">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwRQ">A rare related phenomenon are <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anticrepuscular_rays" title="Anticrepuscular rays" id="mwRg">anticrepuscular rays</a> which can appear at the same time (and coloration) as crepuscular rays but in the opposite direction to the setting sun (east rather than west).</p>
